title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure (IaC), model-serving, observability, performance SLAs, and the ADR process. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers and architects when designing new services or changing existing systems.

Principles:
- Consistency: APIs, observability, and deployment patterns must be predictable across services.
- Safety: Changes must protect customer data, availability, and performance.
- Measurability: Every production service must expose metrics, logs, and traces that support SLOs and incident triage.
- Backwards-compatibility: Use semantic versioning and clear migration plans for public-facing APIs.
- Cost-awareness: Design for predictable unit economics (batching, caching, appropriate hardware sizing).

1) API Standards (Design + Versioning + Errors)
- API style: Use RESTful JSON over HTTPS for public/internal HTTP APIs. For high-throughput streaming/text generation use gRPC or HTTP/2 streaming endpoints where supported.
- Base patterns: every API must document: path, method, request schema, response schema, auth, rate limits, example requests/responses, and common errors. Store schemas in the central API catalog (service: api-catalog).
- Versioning: Semantic versioning for API surfaces. v1 -> v2 migration requires an ADR and a migration/compatibility window (minimum 90 days for public endpoints). Support feature flags for gradual rollout.
- Error model: Use standard HTTP codes. Body includes { "code": string, "message": string, "details": optional object }. Public error codes must be enumerated in docs.
- Rate limiting: Default per-account policy: 1200 requests/minute for host-level endpoints; override per product need. All rate-limit headers must conform to: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
- Authentication: Bearer token (Authorization: Bearer <token>). For private deployments, mutual TLS can be required as specified in deployment config.
- OpenAPI: All HTTP APIs must publish an OpenAPI 3.0 spec and include examples. Specs live in git service: api-specs repo.

2) Coding Standards
- Languages & frameworks: primary backend languages are Go (for high-throughput services) and Python (for orchestration, evals, data pipelines). Use company-approved frameworks: go-std-http + chi/router and internal infra-sdk; python services use FastAPI for HTTP + pydantic for schemas.
- Formatting & linting: Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff/mypy for Python. CI must block merges on lint or type-check failures.
- Testing: Unit tests + integration tests + a smoke test. Service-level test coverage target: >= 70% for business logic code. Use testcontainers or staging infra for integration tests that require GPUs or model runtime.
- PR practices: Max PR size ~ 400 lines of code when possible; require at least one code owner review and one cross-team reviewer for infra/API changes.
- Dependency management: Use go.mod and pip-tools/poetry. Vulnerability scans run in CI; any critical CVE must be remediated within 7 days or an exception ADR created.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC, Security, Networking)
- IaC: Terraform v1.x modules (registry: tf-redwood) for all cloud resources. Every environment (dev/staging/prod) must be represented as Terraform workspaces with specified state backend (S3 + DynamoDB locking for AWS).
- Naming & tagging: All cloud resources must include tags: service, owner, environment, cost-center. Example: {service="redwood-serving",owner="ml-platform",environment="prod",cost-center="ai-prod"}.
- Secrets & KMS: Use centralized secrets manager (Vault / AWS Secrets Manager). Customer keys for private deployments must support BYOK via KMS/HSM integration.
- Networking: VPC design must follow the reference architecture: private subnets for inference clusters, dedicated management subnets for control plane. Use least-privilege security groups and egress filters for private deployments per policy.
- Capacity & autoscaling: Use target tracking and scheduled scaling for GPU pools. Default GPU cluster autoscaling policy: scale when average GPU utilization > 70% for 5m; downscale when < 30% for 10m (adjust per workload after perf validation).

4) Model-Serving Standards
- Packaging: Models must be checked into model registry (service: model-registry) with metadata: model_id, version, architecture, tokenizer, quantization profile, supported sequence lengths, cache incompatibilities.
- Versioning & pinning: Models must be versioned and deployable as immutable artifacts. Customers can pin model_id:version. When rolling changes, keep compatible variants (e.g., float -> quantized) and provide fallback mappings.
- Quantization profiles: Maintain and publish quantization-profiles per model in /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles. Profiles include expected perf delta and accuracy delta at target benchmarks.
- Kernel selection: Runtime will auto-select kernels based on hardware and sequence length but services must document preferred handshake hints (cpu_affinity, preferred_batch_size, max_sequence).
- Routing & fallback: Smart routing policy required: primary model -> fallback to smaller/cheaper variant on capacity constraints or during degraded performance. Implement circuit-breaker with configurable thresholds (default failure rate 5% over 1m triggers fallback to next-tier model).
- Input validation: Enforce token limits, sanitization, and request size checks at API gateway to protect runtime. Return 413 for payloads exceeding limits.

5) Observability Standards (Metrics, Logs, Traces)
- Metrics: Use Prometheus format. Required metrics for service: request_count{route,method,status}, request_latency_ms{p95,p99}, token_generation_latency_ms, model_inference_time_ms, gpu_memory_util_bytes, batch_size_distribution.
- Naming conventions: metric names use snake_case and include service prefix: redwood_<service>_<metric>. Labels must include service, environment, model_id (when applicable), route.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing. Span naming convention: <service>.<operation>. Propagate trace context across internal RPCs and into model runtime.
- Logs: Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, request_id, user_id (if applicable), model_id, message, error_stack. Sensitive data must be redacted before writing logs.
- Dashboards & Alerts: Every owned service must provide a dashboard with SLO panels and on-call runbook links. Alerting: critical pages (P1) for SLO breach must notify on-call via PagerDuty.

SLOs & Alerting (table):
Metric | SLO | Alert threshold | Owner
------|-----|----------------|------
API success rate (per-customer) | 99.95% (30d) | 99.8% (1h) | infra-platform
P95 latency (text-generation) | <= 250ms (regional cached) | > 400ms (5m) | serving-runtime
P99 latency | <= 1200ms | > 1800ms (5m) | serving-runtime
GPU OOM rate | < 0.1% | > 0.5% (1d) | eng-infra

Retention & sampling: traces retained 30 days, metrics retained 365 days (downsampled), logs retained 90 days by default. High-cardinality debug logs may be routed to short-term storage with links in dashboards.

6) Performance Standards & Benchmarking
- Benchmarks: All serving models must have a published perf profile with throughput (tokens/sec), latency (P50/P95/P99), and cost-per-token at target hardware. Benchmarks must be run with realistic prompt distribution (sampled from production or representative workloads).
- Load testing: Use staging clusters with synthetic traffic that mimics production distribution. Run pre-deploy canary tests: 1% traffic for 30 minutes (smoke), 10% for 2 hours (load), then ramp.
- Performance regressions: Any change that increases median token latency by >10% or increases cost-per-token by >8% requires an ADR and rollback or optimization plan.

7) Decision Records (ADRs)
- Purpose: ADRs capture architectural decisions that are non-trivial and affect multiple teams or long-term behavior.
- Template: 
  - ADR ID (e.g., ADR-2026-01)
  - Title
  - Status (proposed | accepted | deprecated)
  - Context
  - Decision
  - Consequences (operational, costs, migration)
  - Owner
  - Date
- Where to store: ADRs live in the confluence/architecture-and-standards ADR index and in git repo: infra-adr/adr-files.
- Process: Proposed ADRs must have at least two reviewers from affected teams, and be discussed in the architecture review channel. For major decisions (affecting infra or public API), presentation at the weekly architecture forum is required.

Example recent ADRs (summary):
- ADR-2026-01: Unified Serving API v2 - accepted 2026-01-12 - Introduced a unified request/response envelope for latency-optimized streaming and batch inference. Owner: Marco Ruiz.
- ADR-2025-09: Quantization Profiles Standard - accepted 2025-09-30 - Defined schema for quantization profiles and validation tests in model-registry. Owner: Chen Li.

8) Change & Rollout Playbook (short)
1. Create change in feature branch and update OpenAPI/schema.
2. Add/update unit & integration tests and perf tests.
3. Run CI including benchmarks (local/staging).
4. Create ADR if crossing thresholds (API shape, infra, perf).
5. Deploy to canary: 1% traffic for 30 minutes. Monitor SLOs and dashboard.
6. If no regressions, ramp to 10% for 2 hours.
7. Full rollout with monitoring and automatic rollback on predefined thresholds (e.g., P95 latency > 20% baseline or error rate increase > 2x).

Ownership & Contacts:
- Architecture review board: arch-board@redwood.internal (chairs: Aisha Patel, Marco Ruiz).
- Serving runtime & performance: eng-serving-runtime (owner: Chen Li).
- Infra & provisioning: eng-infra (owner: Priya Nair).
- API design & docs: eng-developer-experience (owner: Olivia Grant).

Appendices / Links:
- Model registry docs: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding
- Quant profiles: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles
- ADR index: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-index
- API spec repo: git@internal:redwood/api-specs.git

If anything in this standard conflicts with security or legal directives, follow the tighter control. For clarifications or proposed changes, open an ADR and assign to the architecture review board.
